questions.q: The DevOps, Testing & Deployment course's Source Control Integration and CI/CD lessons answered which question?
options: How a change technically gets from a developer's sandbox to production through a version-controlled pipeline
How often an organization's teams should release to production
Which teams are allowed to own scoped applications
When ServiceNow will deprecate a given API
questions.explain: Those lessons covered the mechanics of getting a change out via source control and CI/CD — a different question from how often releases should happen organization-wide.

questions.q: Why is release cadence described in this lesson as an architecture decision rather than a tooling decision?
options: Because deciding how frequently customizations ship, and how that interacts with other teams and the upgrade calendar, is a planning and coordination problem, not a matter of which CI/CD tool is used
Because only the CI/CD tool itself determines how often code can be released
Because tooling decisions are always more important than planning decisions
Because release cadence has no real impact on the platform upgrade calendar
questions.explain: The tools (source control, CI/CD pipelines) enable releasing; deciding how often, and coordinating that across teams and the upgrade calendar, is the architecture-level problem.

questions.q: In the three-team scenario, why does Team A shipping weekly straight through the upgrade testing window create a real problem?
options: The pre-upgrade sandbox stops being a stable baseline, since new changes keep landing on top of what the upgrade validation is testing against
Weekly releases are inherently against ServiceNow policy
Team A's cadence is simply wrong and should be changed permanently
It creates no actual problem since each team's changes are isolated by scope
questions.explain: A moving target undermines the whole point of validating against a stable pre-upgrade sandbox — every week changes the baseline being tested.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend instead of forcing every team onto one team's release cadence?
options: A negotiated, shared release calendar with a defined change freeze window around upgrades, built with input from every team
Mandating that every team adopt Team A's weekly cadence permanently
Eliminating release cadences entirely and releasing only during platform upgrades
Letting each team release whenever it wants with no shared visibility at all
questions.explain: A shared, negotiated calendar with a defined freeze window accounts for every team's real delivery needs, rather than optimizing for one team at the expense of others.

questions.q: Why would a change freeze window that only ever lands on one team's schedule be a governance problem, even if it's technically correct?
options: It would quietly erode trust in the governance process over time, since the burden isn't shared across teams
It would have no effect on trust since freeze windows are purely technical
It would make that team's releases technically impossible going forward
It would automatically violate ServiceNow's own release policy
questions.explain: Fairness in governance matters as much as technical correctness — a freeze that always burdens the same team undermines buy-in even when the calendar logic is sound.
